reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / NCCN & genetics references
clinicalPearls: Caused predominantly by germline variants in PTCH1 (and less commonly SUFU or PTCH2), disrupting the Hedgehog signalling pathway, inherited autosomal dominantly
Characterised by multiple basal cell carcinomas developing from a young age, often numerous and appearing across sun-exposed and non-exposed skin
Odontogenic keratocysts of the jaw are a common early feature and may present with jaw swelling or be found on dental imaging
Palmar and plantar pits are a characteristic minor sign supporting the diagnosis
Skeletal and developmental anomalies include bifid or fused ribs, calcification of the falx cerebri, macrocephaly, and characteristic facies
Childhood medulloblastoma occurs in a minority, particularly in SUFU-related disease, and is an important early malignancy to consider
Patients are exquisitely sensitive to ionising radiation, which can induce large numbers of basal cell carcinomas within irradiated fields, so radiotherapy is avoided where possible

Management combines sun protection, regular dermatological surveillance and treatment of skin lesions, dental follow-up for keratocysts, and consideration of Hedgehog pathway inhibitors for extensive disease
reference.pathophysiology: PTCH1 encodes a receptor that normally suppresses the Hedgehog signalling pathway by inhibiting Smoothened. Loss of PTCH1 function (or loss of SUFU, a downstream inhibitor) releases this restraint, causing constitutive Hedgehog pathway activation that drives proliferation in skin basal cells, cerebellar precursors, and other tissues. This produces the multiple basal cell carcinomas, odontogenic keratocysts, developmental anomalies, and predisposition to medulloblastoma, and explains the therapeutic role of Smoothened inhibitors.
additionalDifferentials: Sporadic multiple basal cell carcinomas from chronic sun exposure
Xeroderma pigmentosum and other photosensitivity-related skin cancer syndromes
Bazex-Dupre-Christol and Rombo syndromes (follicular/skin cancer syndromes)
Cowden and other hamartoma tumour syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Germline PTCH1/SUFU sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis with genetic counselling
Regular full-skin dermatological examination for basal cell carcinomas
Dental panoramic (orthopantomogram) imaging for odontogenic keratocysts
Skeletal survey or targeted imaging for characteristic bony anomalies and falx calcification
Brain MRI surveillance for medulloblastoma in young children, especially SUFU carriers, avoiding unnecessary ionising radiation
redFlags: Rapid appearance of numerous basal cell carcinomas, particularly after radiation exposure
Neurological symptoms in a young child suggesting medulloblastoma
Expanding jaw swelling or pathological features from an odontogenic keratocyst
Aggressive or locally invasive basal cell carcinoma requiring specialist management
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is often near normal because basal cell carcinomas rarely metastasise, but cumulative skin tumour burden causes significant morbidity and disfigurement, and childhood medulloblastoma is a serious threat in affected individuals. Careful avoidance of ionising radiation and lifelong dermatological surveillance are central to a good outcome.
pitfalls: Using radiotherapy for skin or other tumours, which can trigger extensive basal cell carcinoma formation
Attributing multiple basal cell carcinomas in a young patient to sun exposure alone
Overlooking odontogenic keratocysts and palmar/plantar pits as diagnostic clues
Failing to consider medulloblastoma risk and appropriate surveillance in young children
